scenes.title: The First Day
scenes.text:
Kindergarten registration opens in March. The district has already decided which school {name} will attend, based on the family's address.

There are other options, if the family wants to try them. A magnet school across town admits students by lottery, and its bus leaves before seven. Homeschooling is legal and free, but it needs a parent at home all day to teach.

{name}, for {poss} part, mostly wants to know whether there will be a class pet.

textVariants.append: The assigned school lost two teachers last year and hasn't replaced them.
The assigned school's parent association raised money for a new science lab.

choices.label: {Subj} goes to the assigned public school
choices.description: Close to home, with kids from the neighborhood.

choices.label: The family enters the magnet school lottery
choices.description: A longer bus ride and a chance at a specialized program.
choices.authorFlag: Magnet lottery odds (0.3) are a placeholder.

choices.label: A parent homeschools {obj}
choices.description: Lessons at the kitchen table, on {poss} own schedule.

availability.reason: No parent is home during the day to teach {obj}

scenes.title: The Magnet Lottery
scenes.textIfSuccess: {name}'s number comes up. The magnet school has a robotics room, a garden, and a bus that leaves at 6:50 in the morning. {name} falls asleep on it most days and doesn't mind.
scenes.textIfFailure: {name}'s number doesn't come up. In August, {subj} starts at the neighborhood school with half the kids from {poss} street, which has its own advantages.

scenes.title: After Three O'Clock
scenes.text:
{name} is eight, and the hours after school are up for grabs. A flyer for a youth soccer league comes home in {poss} backpack: a registration fee, a uniform, and Saturday games two towns over. A neighbor gives piano lessons on Wednesdays. The library runs a free building club, and a teacher keeps a chess club going in the cafeteria.

Then there's the street, or the backyard, or the creek at the end of the block, where kids have been inventing games for free since long before anyone made them a schedule.

And there are the younger kids at home, who get out at 2:45 and can't walk home alone.

choices.label: {Subj} joins a youth sports league
choices.description: Registration, a uniform, and Saturday games, some of them out of town.

availability.stretchNote: Families earning under $50,000 spend about {stat:youth_sports_spending_low_income} a year on a child's main sport; families earning $100,000 or more spend about {stat:youth_sports_spending_high_income}.

choices.authorFlag: Stretch for the two lowest brackets, as at D7; the survey has no league price.
choices.outcome: {name} plays every position badly and loves all of them. Saturday mornings smell like cut grass and orange slices.

choices.label: {Subj} starts music lessons
choices.description: Lessons every week with a neighbor, and an instrument to rent or buy.
choices.authorFlag: No source for the price of music lessons, so this option has no cost check.
choices.outcome: {name} practices scales at the kitchen table, loudly. By spring {subj} can play one whole song, and the whole family can hum it.

choices.label: {Subj} joins the free clubs at school and the library
choices.description: Chess in the cafeteria, building club at the library, no fees.
choices.outcome: {name} learns that a knight moves in an L, and that the librarian saves the best pieces for the regulars.

choices.label: {Subj} spends afternoons playing outside with the neighborhood kids
choices.description: No schedule, no fees, no adults keeping score.
choices.outcome: The neighborhood kids invent a game with a ball, a fence, and rules that change every day. {name} is home when the streetlights come on.

choices.label: {Subj} helps watch the younger kids after school
choices.description: Someone has to be home until the grown-ups get off work.
choices.outcome: {name} learns to make snacks, find lost shoes, and keep a four-year-old out of the street. It's a job, even if nobody calls it one.

researchNote.title: School Funding
researchNote.text: Many public schools are funded partly by local property taxes, so spending per student depends on where a family can afford to live. A large study found that raising per-pupil spending by 10% in every year of school led to {stat:school_spending_effect} higher adult wages, with much larger effects for children from low-income families.
